content: The document outlines detailed guidelines and recommendations for the use of antiretroviral drugs in the treatment and prevention of HIV infection. It includes specific information on drug dosages, testing strategies, and management protocols for various populations, including adults, adolescents, pregnant women, breastfeeding mothers, and children. Key Highlights: 1. Conflict of Interest Declarations: Several experts and institutions involved in the development of these guidelines have declared their potential conflicts of interest. For example: Jessica Haberer (Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard University, USA) disclosed consulting work for organizations such as FHI 360, WHO, and the US National Institutes of Health, with financial compensation. Sarah Huffam (National Centre for HIV/AIDS, Cambodia) was employed as a consultant to write national HIV management guidelines. Anton Pozniak (Chelsea and Westminster NHS Foundation Trust, UK) disclosed research support from pharmaceutical companies and participation in guideline committees. Iryna Zablotska (Kirby Institute, Australia) received research support from Gilead and medication supplies for a PrEP demonstration study. 2. Testing Strategies for HIV Diagnosis: High-Prevalence Settings: A stepwise testing algorithm is recommended, involving initial tests (A1 and A2) and confirmatory tests (A3) in cases of discordant results. Retesting is advised in 14 days for inconclusive results. Low-Prevalence Settings: Early Infant Diagnosis: Testing in infants under 18 months involves nucleic acid testing (NAT) at birth and follow-up testing to confirm results. ART should be initiated immediately if HIV is detected, with retesting to confirm infection. 3. Management of HIV in Pregnant and Breastfeeding Women: The WHO recommends lifelong ART for all pregnant and breastfeeding women living with HIV. A readiness assessment checklist is provided to help countries transition to this approach, addressing national policy and facility-level preparedness. 4. Clinical Staging and Conditions Associated with HIV: Clinical stages 3 and 4 include severe conditions such as HIV wasting syndrome, recurrent bacterial infections, Kaposi sarcoma, and cryptococcal meningitis. Specific conditions like endemic mycoses, HIV-associated nephropathy, and invasive cervical carcinoma are also highlighted. 5. Antiretroviral Drug Dosages: Detailed dosing recommendations are provided for various drug classes, including nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs), non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs), protease inhibitors (PIs), and integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs). For example, abacavir (ABC) is dosed at 300 mg twice daily or 600 mg once daily, while tenofovir (TDF) is dosed at 300 mg once daily. 6. Special Considerations for Children: Weight-based dosing is emphasized for infants and children, with simplified dosing tables provided for ease of implementation. Fixed-dose combinations are preferred, and oral liquid formulations are discouraged unless necessary. Dispersible tablets are recommended as they can be converted into liquid at the point of use. 7. Early Treatment in Newborns: ART initiation in newborns under 4 weeks of age is encouraged to reduce early mortality. However, dosing for preterm infants remains challenging due to limited pharmacokinetic data. 8. Guidance for National Programs: Simplified dosing schedules will be regularly reviewed and updated as new data and formulations become available. 9. General Principles for ARV Use: Age-appropriate fixed-dose combinations are preferred. Dispersible tablets are recommended over oral liquids for their practicality and ease of use. This comprehensive guidance aims to standardize and optimize the use of antiretroviral drugs globally, ensuring effective treatment and prevention of HIV across diverse populations and settings.
